lesson.title: Build Your Body
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 4, Session 3
lesson.footer: Persuasive Writing | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 4 Session 3

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LA04 using the starting point of a paragraph to give prominence to the message and guide the reader; VC2E5LY10 creating texts with elaborated, sequenced ideas; VC2E5LA02 authoritative sources
plan.shape: skim, pick, link, draft: the skim test shows why first sentences matter, students pick topic sentences and linking words, then draft two body paragraphs, because sustained drafting time is the priority this week
plan.criticalFeature: the first sentence of a paragraph tells the reader its claim; the linking word tells them where they are
decisionPoints: the Find the topic sentence round
the choice check: the strongest topic sentence
the exit board: a topic sentence written for a new paragraph
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. One paragraph, all three moves, claim first.
plan.catchUp: Missed the planning? Five minutes with the planner and the Paragraph Builder; draft one body paragraph today.

studentTools: Big piece plan and the introduction draft
Arctic Fact Cards and Power Word Bank
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: Linking words by job: next reason (In addition), strongest (Most importantly), result (As a result), example (For example)
Paragraph recipe: topic sentence, proof, This means..., sell it

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: sort topic sentences from proof, link paragraphs, fix a squashed paragraph, then plan your body paragraphs.
resources.title: Build Your Body
resources.subtitle: The first sentence carries the claim.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences: TOPIC SENTENCE or PROOF.
cards: Every classroom needs a water filter.
Last week the oval flooded twice.
Tap water costs far less than bottled.
Kids should help plan the canteen menu.
Most kids finish lunch in ten minutes.
Our survey: 20 of 25 kids skip canteen food.

TOPIC SENTENCE: Every classroom needs a water filter.
Kids should help plan the canteen menu.
PROOF: Last week the oval flooded twice.
Tap water costs far less than bottled.
Most kids finish lunch in ten minutes.
Our survey: 20 of 25 kids skip canteen food.

steps: Choose a linking word for that job

items.prompt: Write a linking word for each job.
rows: ___, shade protects us from UV. (first reason)
The oval flooded. ___, sport was cancelled. (a result)
Bikes save money. ___, a bus pass costs $300. (an example)
answers: ___, shade protects us from UV. (first reason)
The oval flooded. ___, sport was cancelled. (a result)
Bikes save money. ___, a bus pass costs $300. (an example)

steps: Find where the second reason starts
Give it its own topic sentence
example.answer: Split it, and give the second reason a topic sentence.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest topic sentence for a paragraph about noise?
options: Leaf blowers should be banned before 8 am.
items.explain: It makes a clear claim the paragraph can prove.

items.prompt: Sam squashed two reasons together. Find the problem and fix it.
work: Firstly, dogs need exercise. Also the park has no fence, and cars are dangerous for dogs.
items.answer: Two reasons in one paragraph. Fix: keep exercise here; start a new paragraph: In addition, a fence would keep dogs safe from cars.

example.answer: Firstly, polar bears need more space than any zoo can give. Proof: they roam hundreds of km.

items.prompt: Plan each body paragraph. Then draft them in your writing book, every second line.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: improve weak topic sentences, then explain proof with This means.
resources.title: Paragraph Power
resources.subtitle: Make every paragraph pull its weight.

example.prompt: Weak: This paragraph is about trees.
example.answer: Strong: Every playground needs at least ten shade trees.

items.prompt: Rewrite each weak topic sentence as a sharp claim.
rows: I will talk about bins now.
Phones are a thing at school.
answers: I will talk about bins now.
Every classroom must have a recycling bin.
Phones are a thing at school.
Phones should stay in bags until home time.
Most importantly, shade protects us from skin cancer.

example.prompt: Proof: the oval flooded twice last week.
steps: Say why it matters to the reader
example.answer: This means students lose sport, so the drains must be fixed.

items.prompt: Choose one proof sentence from your draft. Write two different This means... sentences for it. Which is stronger, and why?
items.answer: Two explanations, one chosen, with a reason linked to the reader.

resources.description: Supported option: picture-clue choices, a first link done and a paragraph frame.
resources.title: Paragraph Builder
resources.subtitle: Topic sentence, proof, This means, sell it.

items.hint: The first one is done for you.

example.answer: Firstly, bears need space. According to scientists, they roam hundreds of km. This means zoos are too small.

items.prompt: Build one paragraph: Firstly, ___. According to ___, ___. This means ___.
items.answer: A topic sentence, sourced proof and an explanation.

slides.notes: Open the session. One line: today you build the body of your argument, one strong paragraph at a time.
Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for those who need it. Drafts go in writing books, every second line.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to write body paragraphs that lead with a clear topic sentence.
successCriteria: I can find the topic sentence of a paragraph.
I can write a body paragraph that claims it, proves it and sells it.
I can use linking words to guide my reader between paragraphs.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Today is the longest writing time of the week. Let's make every paragraph count.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Finding the topic sentence is where we start.
Writing a full claim-prove-sell paragraph is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 finding the topic sentence is reachable for all; SC2 the full paragraph is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 linking words is the stretch.

slides.title: The skim test
lines: Busy readers often read only the first sentence of each paragraph.
There are lots of things to think about with zoos.
Polar bears need far more space than any zoo can give.

notes.answer: the second - it tells you the paragraph's claim straight away
beats: SAY: A busy zoo director skims.
They read the first sentence of each paragraph, then decide. Here are two.
ASK: Which first sentence tells the director what the paragraph proves? First or second?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, 1 or 2... show me.
EXPECT: 2
ASK: What does the director learn from the first one?
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: nothing; it could be about anything
SAY: So your first sentence must carry your claim.
trap: thinking the first one is a good hook.
Fix: say hooks start the whole piece; a paragraph starts with its claim.
notes.prep: Launch links to the Week 2 claim-prove-sell paragraph. 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: The first sentence of a paragraph. It says what the paragraph will prove.
slides.example: Polar bears are built for the cold, not an Australian summer.

notes.answer: the first sentence; it says what the paragraph will prove
beats: POINT to the words. SAY: Topic sentence. Say it with me. Topic sentence.
SAY: It's the pin that holds the paragraph in place.
Everything after it proves it.
ASK: What will the example paragraph prove?
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: that polar bears suffer in hot places
trap: a topic sentence that asks a question with no claim.
Fix: student turns the question into a statement with high modality.
notes.prep: Plain-words version of VC2E5LA04: the start of the paragraph gives the message prominence.

slides.title: Watch me build a body paragraph
slides.extract: Firstly, polar bears need far more space than any zoo can give. In the wild, a polar bear can roam hundreds of kilometres in a season. Even a large zoo enclosure is a tiny fraction of that. This means a zoo bear spends its whole life in a space smaller than one day's walk. No animal built to wander should live behind a wall.
highlights: Firstly, polar bears need far more space
In the wild, a polar bear can roam
slides.source: Model letter, written for this session

notes.answer: linking word, topic sentence, proof, This means, sell
beats: POINT to Firstly.
SAY: Linking word tells the director: reason one. Then my claim, straight away.
POINT to In the wild.
SAY: Proof. Then I compare it with a zoo so the gap is obvious.
POINT to This means.
SAY: This means: I explain why the proof matters. Many writers skip this.
ASK: Which sentence sells it? Read it with me.
3 sec. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
EXPECT: No animal built to wander should live behind a wall.
trap: proof dropped in with no explaining sentence.
Fix: student adds This means... after every piece of proof.
notes.stretch: Use As a result instead of This means.
notes.help: Paragraph Builder: four steps, one at a time.
notes.prep: Model body paragraph, continuing the zoo letter. Critical feature: the first sentence carries the claim.

slides.title: Find the topic sentence
slides.pivot: ask which sentence the others are proving
slides.followUp: cold call one student: how did you know?

items.text: A: It also keeps us calm. B: A class pet teaches responsibility. C: Feeding it is a shared job.
A: Plastic straws should be banned. B: They last hundreds of years. C: Paper ones work fine.
A: Our oval floods every winter. B: Kids slip and get hurt. C: The oval needs better drains.
items.answer: C - the claim; A and B prove it
items.say: C. The claim was last here. In your writing, it goes first. Tick or fix.

items.text: A: Shade cuts sunburn risk. B: Every playground needs more trees. C: Trees also cool the air.

say: Three sentences from one paragraph, jumbled.
Point to the one that should go first.
trap: Fix: ask which one do the others prove? Student re-points.
notes.stretch: Add a This means... sentence to each.
notes.help: Look for should, must or need: that's often the claim.
notes.prep: Guided practice on SC1 with mixed orders (megaprompt 19a). SC1.

slides.title: Which is the strongest topic sentence?

options.text: Zoos can be very interesting places to visit.
options.misconception: vague; doesn't say what the paragraph proves

options.text: Polar bears are built for the cold, not for hot summers.
In 2011, scientists tracked a bear swimming for nine days.
options.misconception: a piece of proof, not a claim

notes.answer: B - it claims exactly what the paragraph will prove
beats: SAY: Three possible first sentences for a paragraph about heat.
ASK: Which is the strongest topic sentence?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: where would C go in the paragraph?
Less -> run the skim test on each, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. Skim it and you know what the paragraph proves.
trap: pointing to C because facts are strong.
Fix: ask is it proof or a claim? Student moves it to the middle.
notes.prep: Decision point before drafting. Under 80% means every student writes topic sentence 1 on a board for checking first.

slides.title: Link it
slides.pivot: read the linking words by job on the board
slides.followUp: cold call one board: what job does your linking word do?

items.text: ___, the money spent on zoo bears could protect wild ones. (my strongest reason)
___, polar bears are built for the cold. (my second reason)
Bears pace their enclosures. ___, many zoos now add toys and puzzles. (a result)
items.expect: As a result. ACCEPT: Because of this

items.text: Bears roam huge distances. ___, one swam for nine days. (an example)

say: Each gap needs a linking word.
The brackets tell you its job.
trap: using And then for every link.
Fix: student reads the job in brackets and picks from the board.
notes.stretch: Find two linking words for each job.
notes.help: Match the bracket to the board list.

slides.title: Draft your body paragraphs
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet, plan each paragraph, then draft your body paragraphs in your writing book.
slides.visualLabel: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it.

notes.answer: two or three body paragraphs, each led by its claim
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Aim for two paragraphs today. Three if you're flying.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CONFERENCE with exit-list students first. Read only their topic sentences.
ASK: How many body paragraphs are finished?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: 1 at 12 minutes, 2 by the end
TIME 22 minutes. At 18, partners do the skim test on each other.
trap: two reasons squashed into one paragraph.
Fix: student draws a line between them and adds a new topic sentence.
notes.stretch: Extension: sharpen weak topic sentences and explain proof two ways.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet (Paragraph Builder): picture-clue choices, a first link done, a frame.
notes.prep: Independent drafting, the longest writing block of the week. SC2 and SC3.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in a paragraph plan, then two or three drafted body paragraphs

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Walking gets your heart pumping before class. It's free, and you can chat with friends on the way.
Write the topic sentence that should start this paragraph.

notes.answer: e.g. Walking is the best way to start a school day
beats: SAY: A paragraph with no first sentence. Give it one.
ASK: Write the topic sentence.
45 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: a claim that walking to school is good, with high modality
RECORD who writes a fact or a question. Tomorrow's conference.
trap: Did you know walking is good?
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 (leading with the claim) on a new topic. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Read only your topic sentences to your partner. Can they guess your whole argument?

notes.answer: open - the topic sentences alone should carry the argument
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that your paragraphs lead with their claim?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: Read only your topic sentences. Can your partner guess your argument?
30 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: yes, they could say my reasons back
notes.prep: Self-assessment and the skim test on their own work. SC2.
